body:
You are drafting spoken lines for a video game. Reply with plain text only, in the exact row format given at the end of this message. Do not send messages to anyone else and do not ask questions: decide. Write nothing but the rows (no title, no notes, no Markdown).

THE GAME. "The Crooked Moon" is a single-player, turn-based tactical party RPG built from a folk-horror Dungeons and Dragons campaign. It is set in Wickermoor Hollow, a haunted valley in Druskenvald, a land of endless night under a giant Crooked Moon with a crone's face. The look is a Halloween that never ends, drawn like an 1980s cartoon. A ghost train, the Ghostlight Express, has crashed in the valley; the party is stranded in the Hollow and its village, Wickermoor. The tone is warm, wry and funny on the surface, with real dread and real grief underneath. The player controls a party of four chosen from six companions: Rook Coldwake, Tobin Hayward, Silas Vane, Delphine Ravelle, Lucan Houndstooth and Cordelia Skein. They are quirky, capable adults.

THE NARRATOR. A NARRATOR row is spoken by the Vagrant, the green-skinned ferryman of the ghost train, who tells the tale in a folksy Southern drawl. At the camp fire he is warm and wry, and when a talk turns sad his humour leaves and he goes plain and level. He speaks to the party as "you" and about the companion in the third person, by first name. Present tense, one or two sentences, under about 32 words. Concrete senses (a smell, a sound, a touch, what the hands are doing) over adjectives. Never tell the player what to feel. Never "suddenly". No facts the party could not see. Drop the final g ("hangin'") in about one Narrator row in four, and use no other dialect spelling. He is kind, never mocks a stumble and never makes light of the dead.

RULES FOR EVERY LINE.
1. The companion's voice sheet below comes first. Match its accent, pace, vocabulary and contractions, and the existing lines. Use a pet phrase at most twice in the whole reply and never twice in one talk. Never repeat or closely paraphrase a line already in the voice sheet or the note.
2. A SAY row is the companion speaking: one or two short sentences, under about 28 words. Never put three sentences in one row; start another row instead.
3. The party's options (OPTION rows) are under 12 words, in the plain voice of the party, work at any hour and in any weather, never name a hero, and are never rolls or checks. A reply must always answer the option it follows.
4. Canon limits. Use only the facts in the voice sheet and the note below. Do not invent a new named person, place, monster, event, object the companion carries, or piece of the companion's history. You may invent small, harmless habits, fondnesses, superstitions and turns of phrase, and the look of the fire and the night. Name no place that the note does not name. Never state a dark secret. You may come close to one and step back.
5. Nothing here is a game system: no dice, no checks, no points, no levels, no HP, no "approval", no menus talked about aloud. Plain punctuation only (commas, full stops, hyphens, apostrophes, question marks, quotation marks inside a line when someone is quoted). No em dashes, no semicolons, no brackets, no asterisks, no stage directions, no placeholders.
6. Humour comes from the character, never explained. The sad turn is plain and short.
7. Our own words. Nothing quoted from any book.

THIS REQUEST. Four camp talks about Silas's personal story, the Thread of Liberation. The companion is SILAS VANE (call them Silas in NARRATOR rows). The attached note is the voice sheet and the fact sheet; it describes an older plan for the Thread's beats in places, so take people, objects, manner and background from it, but where it disagrees with THE FIXED FACTS in this brief, the fixed facts win.

HOW A CAMP TALK WORKS. After a rest the player can walk up to a companion who has asked for a word at the fire. It is private, short and warm. The companion speaks first (NARRATOR and SAY rows), the player chooses what the party says from three short options (or two where the talk says so), and the companion answers in their own voice (a REPLY). Then the talk ends. Nothing in it is a roll or a failure, and every reply must leave the talk finished and the fire going: a cool reply is still an ending, never a slammed door. Each reply also carries a REASON row: one sentence beginning "You", past tense, under 14 words, saying what the party did or said as the companion would remember it (for example "You heard me out at the fire" or "You waved it off and went to bed"). A REASON is plain notice text and is not spoken.

THE FIXED FACTS (the beats in the game's journal; the talks tell these, in Silas's own words, and go no further than they do).
- Silas's Thread: Silas's Liberation. What Silas wants: Find the loophole in the bet he lost, and win back what he staked.
- The Connection already happened in Wickermoor, with Holly Aster, the baker. The journal says: "Holly Aster kept a page back for Silas, and baked a loaf around it."
- The Discovery, "The Fine Print", happens in the Drowned Crossroads. The journal's line for it: "At the Drowned Crossroads Silas found the table where his bet was taken, and the clause that might undo it."
- The Confrontation, "Calling the Bluff", happens in Fool's Day (the festival). The journal's line for it: "On Fool's Day Silas called the house's bluff, and the small shadow at his heel went quiet."
Each talk is had at camp AFTER its chapter is over, so Silas looks back on what happened. You may name the Drowned Crossroads in the Discovery and Fool's Day (the festival) in the Confrontation and no other place. Do not describe fights, bosses or villains; Silas speaks of what was found, felt or chosen.

THE INCITEMENT AS IT PLAYED (for the first talk). Silas sometimes misses this scene because Silas is not with the party when it plays in the Mariner's car of the Ghostlight Express. Then Silas goes back alone, and at camp tells the party what was found. These are the facts of the scene; do not change them, you may add small sensory detail:
[liberation_start]
  NARRATOR: Burnt sealing wax and cold dock silt hang in the Mail Car air, and Silas freezes after two sharp sniffs. A brass-cornered envelope slips from a torn mailbag and lands face up at his boots, stamped with a grinning skull and spade.
  SILAS: Hold the deal. That wax belongs to a river house that never mails a friendly card.
  NARRATOR: The parchment inside is blank until Silas's lagging shadow leans close, drawing out a dead river-clerk's cramped warning and a sketched table with two empty chairs.
  NARRATOR: A soul can be won back at the Drowned Crossroads if your own shadow helps you cheat, so Silas stuffs wormwood into his censer to blind his creditor's lookout with green smoke.
  SILAS: Easy now, breathe the bitter herb and keep your eyes off the ink, you long-legged snitch. House rules say a man gets to read his own summons before the debt comes due.
  the party can say: Show us what's on that paper, Silas.
  the party can say: Burn the letter before the smoke clears.
  the party can say: Pocket it and keep moving.
[liberation_shown]
  NARRATOR: Silas angles the parchment through the coiling wormwood smoke so you can see the two empty chairs drawn beside the baize. His thumb taps the second seat, and the fast patter drops right out of his voice.
  SILAS: Two chairs means two markers on the ledger, friends, and only one of those fools is standing here in boots. If I sit down at the Drowned Crossroads, I am playing to buy back more than my own hide.
[liberation_burned]
  NARRATOR: Silas flicks his flint-lighter against a brass corner, and the river-clerk's warning curls into black ash that smells of river mud. His lagging shadow twitches on the floorboards, cheated of a second look.
  SILAS: Ash holds no ink, and a blind lookout cannot tattle to the house. I got the table and the stakes in my head, and that is the only place the dealer cannot reach.
[liberation_pocketed]
  NARRATOR: Silas folds the heavy parchment twice and slides it cleanly into the middle of his bone-sliver tarot deck. He gives the pack a one-handed cut and shows his teeth in a crooked grin.
  SILAS: Best place to hide a marked card is right inside a rigged deck. Come on, let us walk before the smoke thins and my shadow remembers who pays its wages.

THE TALKS. Write these four talks, in this order, with these keys.

TALK incitement. Silas tells the party about the Mariner's car of the Ghostlight Express as one short story at the fire. Opening: 1 NARRATOR row, then 3 or 4 SAY rows (the story, in their own words, ending on a plain statement of how it left them). TWO options only: OPTION 1 asks to hear more or says something that shares the moment; OPTION 2 is the quiet way on, leaving Silas to it. Two replies of 1 NARRATOR row (optional) and 1 or 2 SAY rows. No REASON rows in this talk.

TALK discovery. Silas has come back from the Drowned Crossroads with the Discovery, and wants to tell it. Opening: 1 NARRATOR row to open the scene at the fire, then 6 to 8 SAY rows (one more NARRATOR row is allowed in the middle) that tell what the journal line says in Silas's own words and end on the turn: how it sits with them, with one thing left unsaid (never the dark secret: no names, deeds or places from the note's dark-secret section). Three options: OPTION 1 asks Silas to say more; OPTION 2 is the answer most like what Silas would want to hear, meeting Silas on Silas's own terms; OPTION 3 is the quiet way on, civil but brisk, brushing it past. Three replies of 1 to 3 rows each, each ending the talk, each with a REASON row. The cool reply (3) must still leave the Discovery told.

TALK confrontation_wait. Silas is at their lowest regard for the party (Strained), and has the Confrontation to tell about Fool's Day (the festival) but is holding it back until things are mended. This talk is short. Opening: 1 NARRATOR row and 3 or 4 SAY rows: Silas says there is something to say about it and it will keep, and says, in Silas's own voice, what matters to Silas and that the party's way has drifted from it (do not claim any specific deed the party did). Three options: OPTION 1 listens and owns it (the way to mend); OPTION 2 answers coldly; OPTION 3 says nothing and gives Silas room (its option text is plain words such as "Say nothing. Stay by the fire."; this reply has NO REASON row). Replies of 1 or 2 rows. Nothing is lost for good: even the cold reply leaves the door open.

TALK confrontation. Silas's story comes to a head. Opening: 1 NARRATOR row, then 7 to 9 SAY rows (one more NARRATOR row allowed in the middle) that tell what the journal line says in Silas's own words: the heart of their act-three story, plain and a little raw, never grand; Silas may say that something from before has found them, but must NOT name or describe the person, the act or the event behind the dark secret (no names, deeds, places or objects from the note's dark-secret section, or from its Climax and Catharsis sections): say only what it was like to stand one's ground against it; end on the turn and a question or a long silence. Three options: OPTION 1 asks Silas to say more; OPTION 2 is the answer most like what Silas needs to hear; OPTION 3 is the quiet way on, brushing it past. Three replies of 1 to 3 rows each, each ending the talk, each with a REASON row. The cool reply must still leave the Confrontation told.

THE ROW FORMAT (exact). One row per line, rows in this order, nothing else:

TALK <key>
NARRATOR: <line>
SAY: <line>
SAY: <line>
OPTION 1: <what the party says>
OPTION 2: <what the party says>
OPTION 3: <what the party says>
REPLY 1
NARRATOR: <optional line>
SAY: <line>
REASON: You <what the party did>
REPLY 2
...
REPLY 3
...

TALK <key> starts a talk (the keys are given below, exactly). The rows before the first OPTION are the talk's opening. Each REPLY block holds one optional NARRATOR row first, then one or two SAY rows, then a REASON row (and an INSPIRE row where the talk asks for one). Write exactly the talks listed, in the order listed, with the row counts given.

The TALK keys, exactly: incitement, discovery, confrontation_wait, confrontation.

ATTACHED DOCUMENTS. Two documents come attached to this message; read both before you write. `tasks/crooked-moon-companions/silas_vane-voice-and-beats.md` holds the voice sheet for SILAS VANE (age, accent, pace, pet phrases, existing lines) and the character file (what Silas likes and dislikes, the Thread, the dark secret you must never state). `tasks/crooked-moon-companions/silas_vane-camp-talks.md` holds the camp talks already written for Silas, as voice examples: do not repeat their topics or lines.
result:
TALK incitement
NARRATOR: Silas crouches near the fire, feedin' dry wormwood stems into his brass censer until a ribbon of green smoke curls round his ribs.
SAY: Doubled back to that wrecked mail car while you lot were catching your breath, friend, and found an old bill waiting in the spilled sacks.
SAY: Brass-cornered envelope with a skull-and-spade seal, blank as bone until my own lagging shadow leaned over the page and drew the ink right out.
SAY: Some dead clerk left a map to a house table where a bad stake can be won back if your own shadow helps you cheat the shoe.
SAY: I have been dodging that tab for years, and holding the paper made my ribs feel ten winters colder.
OPTION 1: Who sent the summons?
OPTION 2: Keep your eyes on the road ahead.
REPLY 1
NARRATOR: Silas taps the edge of his bone tarot deck against his knee, his green eye-lights narrowing through the bitter smoke.
SAY: We call him the Dealer, friend, and he never posts a card unless he expects you to sit down and lose the rest of your skin.
SAY: Still, if there is a crooked table waiting down the line, I would rather bring my own nerve than let his lookout drag me there.
REPLY 2
SAY: Fair play, friend, no sense crying over a marked hand before the cards even hit the baize.
SAY: Just do not mind the extra smoke tonight while I keep my little shadow blind.

TALK discovery
NARRATOR: Silas sits on an upturned crate by the embers, turning a single bone card over his knuckles while his shadow stretches flat and still behind him.
SAY: Walked right into the Drowned Crossroads and found the exact green baize where my old tab was written, friend, still smelling of canal rot and cheap wax.
SAY: Same silver shoe humming on the cloth, same cold ledger waiting to collect, like the house never closed the game after I ran.
SAY: I used to think the Dealer wrote an airtight contract, no exit in the margins, just pay the blood stake or fold.
NARRATOR: He stops the card between two fingerbones and lets out a quick, dry breath through his teeth.
SAY: Then my own spying shadow slipped a card off the bottom of the deck and pointed out the fine print tucked behind the seal.
SAY: Turns out any bet taken at that table can be called back for a straight draw if the house lookout turns partner and backs the player's hand.
SAY: My shadow is dealing for me now, friend, which means the loophole is real and the ledger can actually be opened.
SAY: Only catch is sitting back down at that cloth means looking straight at the marker I left behind when I walked away the first time.
OPTION 1: What else was written on that marker?
OPTION 2: Then we use the loophole and clean out the house.
OPTION 3: You found what you needed. Get some rest.
REPLY 1
NARRATOR: The green pinpoints in Silas's sockets dip toward the ash, and his thumb rubs the front of his breastbone through his waistcoat.
SAY: Just a date and a price that never should have been mine to spend, friend, and that is all the air I am giving it tonight.
SAY: When the time comes to pull that page out of the book, I will make sure the tally comes out clean.
REASON: You asked what else was written on my marker.
REPLY 2
NARRATOR: Silas lets out a short, raspy laugh, snapping the card back into his pack with a one-handed flourish.
SAY: Now that is proper table talk, friend, no trembling over the buy-in when the shoe is finally tipping our way.
SAY: Let the house count its chips for now, because next time we sit down we are taking the whole pot back.
REASON: You backed my play to clean out the house.
REPLY 3
SAY: Right you are, friend, a hustler who stays up admiring his own hand usually gets his pockets picked by dawn.
SAY: I will tuck the clause away and keep my knuckles ready for morning.
REASON: You told me to rest after hearing my news.

TALK confrontation_wait
NARRATOR: Silas stands a few paces back from the firelight, his brass censer hangin' cold on its chain while his jaw clicks once against the damp.
SAY: Something big went down back at Fool's Day, friend, right across the sawdust where the house thought it had me boxed.
SAY: I would lay the whole hand out for you tonight, only I like knowing the people at my elbow will not sell a poor sod's skin to the bailiff.
SAY: Lately your play has been a bit too cozy with bad bargains and tall hats, and I do not show my hole card at a table I cannot read.
SAY: Let us see how we walk the next mile or two before I open my waistcoat on this one.
OPTION 1: Fair enough. We will do better by you.
OPTION 2: Keep your secrets if you want.
OPTION 3: Say nothing. Stay by the fire.
REPLY 1
NARRATOR: Silas loosens his shoulders a fraction and flips a pinch of dry herb into the brass grate.
SAY: Tell's in the twitch, friend, and you sounded straight enough just then.
SAY: Give it a little road dust to settle, and I will tell you how we called the bluff.
REASON: You owned your missteps and promised to do better.
REPLY 2
SAY: Suit yourself, friend, a quiet table saves breath for both of us.
SAY: Card will still be in my pocket if the wind changes and you feel like talking square.
REASON: You told me to keep my secrets to myself.
REPLY 3
NARRATOR: Silas watches the sparks rise into the dark for a beat, then nods once and steps back toward his bedroll.
SAY: Night is long enough without forcing the deal, friend.

TALK confrontation
NARRATOR: Silas sits close to the flames with his brass censer unhooked beside his boots, while the small shadow at his heel lies quiet and still.
SAY: Back at Fool's Day, behind all the sour smoke and painted streamers, the Dealer finally pushed his own voice across the counter to name his price.
SAY: He thought flashing the old ledger in the dark would make me scramble for a dirty trick, same way I did the night my tab began.
SAY: Every hustle I ever pulled was just noise to keep from hearing that first game, friend, when I let the mark fall where it did not belong.
NARRATOR: He rests his bony palms flat on his knees, no cards in his fingers and no patter in his throat.
SAY: House always wins, unless you burn the house, or unless you stop shaking long enough to look the swindler in the eye.
SAY: So I called his bluff flat out across the sawdust and told him to bring the whole ledger to the table when the last hand gets dealt.
SAY: Second I laid the challenge down, the chain on my censer went cold and the little shadow at my heel stopped twitching for its old master.
SAY: No more lookout spying on my sleeve, just me and a straight draw coming for everything I owe.
SAY: Tell me straight, friend, when a gambler throws away his stacked deck, do you reckon he still has a prayer of winning an honest hand?
OPTION 1: What happens when that last hand comes due?
OPTION 2: You will beat him straight, and we will be there.
OPTION 3: Save your strength for the road tomorrow.
REPLY 1
NARRATOR: Silas picks up a glowing coal with two bare fingerbones and drops it into the censer just to watch the warm light.
SAY: Then the pages go down on the cloth, friend, and there is nowhere left to palm a card or hide behind the smoke.
SAY: Either I read his tell with clean hands and walk everybody out of that book, or the tab closes on me for good.
REASON: You asked what comes next when the last hand is dealt.
REPLY 2
NARRATOR: A quick, crooked grin returns to Silas's jaw, and his small shadow raises one hand in a silent salute against the logs.
SAY: Never thought I would hear myself backing an honest draw, friend, but with this crew at the table I might actually like the odds.
SAY: Let the old cheat bring his ledger whenever he is ready, because we are not folding an inch.
REASON: You trusted me to win the final hand straight.
REPLY 3
SAY: Always practical, friend, and here I was getting sentimental over a quiet shadow.
SAY: The bluff is called and the stake is set, so I will take my rest while the brass is cool.
REASON: You kept things brisk and told me to rest.
